title: sms-florin eSIM - WebMCP checkout on a live product
pitch: A live eSIM store with real Stripe billing where an AI browser agent can list plans and start a genuine checkout via two WebMCP tools - the same flow a human uses, no DOM guessing.

 What's next for sms-florin eSIM - WebMCP checkout on a live product 

 Inspiration 

 Most "AI agent buys something on a website" demos are toy stores built for the demo. We wanted to answer a harder question: can WebMCP be dropped onto a real product that already takes real money without rebuilding the checkout, and without opening a security hole? sms-florin sells eSIM data plans with live Stripe billing, so it was the honest test case. 

 What it does 

 The live page flo-voice1.com/esim exposes two WebMCP tools to any WebMCP-aware browser (e.g. ChatGPT Desktop): 

 
 list_esim_plans — returns the live plan catalog: country, data amount, duration, price. 
 buy_esim_plan — takes a plan slug and creates a real Stripe Checkout session, handing the agent the checkout URL. No money moves until a human enters card details on Stripe's own page — the tool starts a real purchase, it doesn't complete a charge on its own. 
 

 An agent can go from "find me a 7-day UK data plan" to a fully-formed Stripe checkout for that exact plan in two tool calls, without ever parsing the page's HTML or clicking a button it had to locate visually. 

 How we built it 

 
 Tool registration : a ~40-line client component calls document.modelContext.registerTool() for the two tools on page mount. It's feature-detected — document.modelContext only exists in a WebMCP-aware browser, so the component is a silent no-op everywhere else and ships to production safely. 
 Backing endpoints : two public, unauthenticated routes — GET /api/v1/esim-catalog (returns the same data the page renders) and POST /api/v1/esim-checkout (creates the Stripe session, returns its URL). 
 Shared checkout path : the Stripe session creation was refactored into one function used by both the human checkout form and the WebMCP endpoint, so the agent and the human get identical pricing, identical metadata, identical guarantees. There is no separate "agent checkout" to drift out of sync. 
 Stack : Next.js (App Router) on the existing production deployment, Stripe Checkout, WebMCP via the browser's document.modelContext API. Deployed as-is on the live site — this is not a separate demo environment. 
 

 Challenges we ran into 

 
 Doing this on a commercial product. The full sms-florin app has live billing and stays closed-source, so we carved out just the WebMCP integration layer (tool component + two routes + the shared checkout lib) into a public MIT repo that still reflects exactly what's deployed. 
 A tool's execute() returns a value; a form action redirects. The human flow does a server-side redirect to Stripe. An agent tool needs a value back, so the endpoint returns the checkout URL as JSON and the tool hands it to the agent instead of navigating server-side. 
 Not opening an abuse surface. The new endpoints are unauthenticated (same guest-checkout model the human form already uses) but IP rate-limited, and buy_esim_plan cannot move money — worst case is a created-but-unpaid Stripe session, which expires on its own. 
 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 WebMCP added to a product that already has paying customers, in hours not days, with one shared code path for humans and agents and no new security hole. The integration is live in production right now, not staged for judging. 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP's surface is genuinely small — no .well-known file, no manifest, no separate server, just document.modelContext.registerTool() client-side. The real design work isn't the protocol, it's deciding which existing actions are safe to expose and making the agent path reuse the human path instead of forking it. 

 What's next for sms-florin eSIM 

 
 Wrap the other live product (UK phone-number rentals) the same way. 
 A check_esim_order_status tool so an agent can follow up on a purchase it started. 
 Declarative <form toolname="..."> variants alongside the JS registration.
